nodes.question: What percentage of Denmark's total national greenhouse gas emissions is attributed to agriculture?
nodes.answer: Agriculture accounts for 24% of the total national greenhouse gas emissions in Denmark.

In a northern European country like Denmark, where 62% of the territorial land is used for agricultural produc- tion (Statistics Denmark 2020) which accounts for 24% of the total national greenhouse gas emissions (Dalgaard et al. 2011) regenerative farming is receiving increased attenton. Radical change in the agrifood system is needed to counter - act the negative effects of post WWII intensifiation and spe- cialization of production, that have led to drastic biodiversity loss (Danish Biodiversity Council 2022), nitrogen leaching to surface waters (Kronvang et al. 2008), a decrease in soil carbon stocks (Adhikari et al. 2014), and very high debt and thus path dependency among farmers (Hansen 2019). Many interpretations of regenerative farming exist side by side, since numerous different actors are increasingly interested in the concept, often with very different visions (Newton et al. 2020; Giller et al. 2021; Kallio and LaFleur 2023). nodes.question: Why do you think there has been a shift towards more consumer-targeted policies for sustainable food choices over time?
nodes.answer: The shift towards more consumer-targeted policies for sustainable food choices may be due to the urgency of climate protection measures and the recognition of agricultural production as a powerful lever in reducing greenhouse gas emissions.

nodes.answer: Factors contributing to greenhouse gas emissions, water, energy, and land use include the consumption of ultra-processed foods, as highlighted in the longitudinal assessment.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Carbon footprint reduction|Sustainable agriculture practices_qna_007
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: How are greenhouse gas emissions, water, energy, and land use impacted by the consumption of ultra-processed foods?
nodes.answer: The consumption of ultra-processed foods has been found to be a promoting factor for greenhouse gas emissions, water consumption, energy use, and land use according to the longitudinal assessment conducted.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Carbon footprint reduction|Sustainable agriculture practices_qna_008
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What trends were observed in the environmental parameters if ultra-processed food consumption increased at baseline and 2-year follow-up?
nodes.answer: Increasing ultra-processed food consumption would lead to higher greenhouse gas emissions and energy use, along with a decrease in water use. A rise in ultra-processed food consumption would result in lower water use and higher energy consumption and CO2 emissions at the 2-year follow-up compared to baseline.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Carbon footprint reduction|Sustainable agriculture practices_qna_009
nodes.label: Ethics and regulation
nodes.question: Why must mitigation practices be evaluated at the whole farm level?
nodes.answer: Mitigation practices that reduce emissions in one stage may increase emissions elsewhere due to system interactions.
nodes.paragraph: The authors highlighted that medium duration (i.e. 18 24 months) grassland-based beef production systems in Scotland were found to achieve a balance between financial returns and environmental performance. A study comprising sites in different nations in the UK (Cardenas et al. 2019) found that NUE depended on the type of N fertiliser, and although NUE increased with fertiliser rate, so did the emis- sions of N2O. Measures such as application of inhibitors and splitting N application were effective in improving NUE in these grasslands. More recently, using qualitative methods, different mitigation measures in the UK agricultural sector were synthesised based on the existing scientific literature and elicitation of expert opinions (Buckingham et al. 2023; Jebari et al. 2023). Nevertheless, due to system interac- tions, mitigation practices that reduce emissions in one stage may increase emissions elsewhere, and mitigation practices must therefore be evaluated at the whole farm level (Montes et al. 2013 ). To the best of our knowl - edge, there have not been studies in the UK investigating multiple mitigation measures via a data-driven scenario analysis with respect to grassland, grazing, and manure management of beef production systems using LCA.

nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What percentage of the EU-28 total greenhouse gas emissions did agriculture account for in 2017?
nodes.answer: Agriculture accounted for 10% of the EU-28 total greenhouse gas emissions in 2017.
nodes.paragraph: HNV High Nature Value PRISMA Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses SAFA Sustainability Assessment of Food and Agri- culture Systems SDGs Sustainable Development Goals UK United Kingdom Introduction Over the last decades, the EU livestock sector has been sub- ject to profound changes regarding its structure, market and environmental conditions, consumer expectation, and regu- lation. Despite these changes and an increasing number of legislative and normative developments, livestock in Europe is still far from a sustainable state (Guyomard et al. 2021). Greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from agriculture made up 10% of the EU-28 total in 2017, and over 80% of agricul- tural GHG emissions are from livestock (ibid.). Regionally concentrated livestock production also leads to water and air pollution, although the total livestock population in the EU declined by 8.9% between 2001 and 2020 (Eurostat 2021). At the same time, livestock farming provides employment on farms and in related sectors, representing 36% of the total EU S agricultural industry's output in 2021, while support- ing food security and human nutrition (Albaladejo Rom n 2023).

nodes.question: What are some of the effects of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions mentioned in the introduction?
nodes.answer: Effects include disturbances to the earth's radiative balance, increased surface temperature, sea level rise, ocean acidification, and impacts on world agriculture.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract In this paper, we analyse the relationship between the rate of growth of CO 2emissions and economic activity in Spain from 1964 to 2020. We explain CO 2emissions by tting a structural regression model with selected indicators of economic activity augmentedwith dynamic common factors extracted from a large macroeconomic database, as explanatory variables. The variables to include in the regression are selected using Machine Learning procedures while we use alternative supervised and non-supervisedprocedures to extract the factors. We nd that, regardless of the procedure used for variable selection, private consumption and maritime transportation have the highest explanatory power for the rate of growth of emissions. We also show that the waythe common factors are extracted is crucial to exploit their information content. The common factors extracted by partial least squares add valuable information on top of that of the selected individual indicators, while they are not signi cant when extractedby two-step-Kalman Iter (2SKF). Keywords Dynamic factor models LASSO Partial least squares V ariable selection 1 Introduction The addition of greenhouse gases (GHG) to the atmosphere disturbs the earth S radia- tive balance, leading to an increase in the earth S surface temperature and to related effects on climate, sea level rise, ocean acidi cation and world agriculture, amongother effects.
